title: Billabong's First Boardshorts, Cut at Home and Sold on Consignment
dek: In 1973 Gordon and Rena Merchant began sewing surf shorts at home on the Gold Coast and grew the business for five years without a loan.

story.event: Making the first boardshorts at home and selling them to Gold Coast surf shops on consignment
story.summary: In 1973 Gordon Merchant, a former surfboard shaper, and Rena Merchant began making boardshorts at home in North Burleigh on the Gold Coast and selling them to local surf shops on consignment at A$4.50 a pair. They added the Billabong name and labels in 1974, opened a small factory in 1975 and, after being refused a business loan in 1977, took their first bank loan of A$7,500 in 1978; sales reached A$1 million in 1981.
paragraphs: In 1972, by Billabong's own history, Rena Merchant was stitching crocheted bikinis and selling them from the back of her van in Angourie, a surf town in northern New South Wales. Her husband, Gordon, born in Sydney in 1943, had surfed since the late 1950s and by the late 1960s was a well-travelled surfboard shaper. In 1973, at home in North Burleigh on Queensland's Gold Coast, the couple began making boardshorts.

The first pair, the company says, was hand-cut from heavy canvas and sewn on the Merchants' kitchen table. A reference-book company history puts that table in a small rented flat; the Encyclopedia of Surfing says the first trunks were made in the basement of their home. The shorts soon moved to a triple stitch and flat thread, so they would survive wipeouts and sit comfortably. The Merchants sold them to Gold Coast surf shops on consignment, at A$4.50 a pair, which meant they were paid only for the pairs that sold. The Encyclopedia of Surfing adds that they also sold shorts from their vehicle as they travelled between surf spots.

The first year brought in about A$5,000 of merchandise, according to the company history in the International Directory of Company Histories. In 1974, at the shops' request, they sewed in labels and chose a name: Billabong, from an Aboriginal word for a creek that runs only in the rainy season, with a wave for its logo. In 1975 they took a 1,000-square-foot factory, and Joe Engel, a Queensland surfer, became the brand's first professional rider.

They paid for growth out of what they sold. By 1977, the same history says, the business was turning over A$100,000 a year and had been incorporated as Gordon & Rena Merchant Pty Ltd, yet it failed to get a business loan. The first bank loan, of A$7,500, came in 1978 and paid for a move into a 7,500-square-foot workshop. Exports to Japan and the United States began in 1979, and annual sales reached A$1 million in 1981.

quote.text: When I was young, my condition was low, and therefore I acquired my ability in many things, but they were mean matters. Must the superior man have such variety of ability? He does not need variety of ability.
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: The Merchants cut, stitched, labelled and sold every pair themselves because there was nobody else to do it. Confucius also learned many humble skills from need, yet would not count that breadth as the mark of a superior person. Whether doing everything is a strength or only a stage stays open.

reflection: In the first years of anything you build, you are cutter, stitcher and salesperson at once. The Merchants did it for five years before a bank would lend them money, and nothing in their record says it was easy.

Confucius was neither proud nor ashamed of the many small skills poverty had taught him; he simply did not mistake them for the point. That may be a kind way to look at your own crowded days. Some of what you do is the work itself. Some of it you do only because nobody else can yet, and it is fair to notice which is which, especially on a tired morning.
invitation: Pick one task you do only because nobody else can yet. Today, write a few plain lines on how you do it, so that one day it can be handed to someone else.

sources.supports: Founded in 1973 at Burleigh Heads by Gordon and Rena Merchant; first boardshorts handmade on the kitchen table and sold locally; triple-stitched seams to withstand wipeouts.

cross_checks.claim: Gordon and Rena Merchant began making boardshorts at home on the Gold Coast in 1973
The first shorts were made at the couple's kitchen table (the Encyclopedia of Surfing says a basement)
The shorts were triple-stitched for durability
Billabong was founded in 1973 and first succeeded with boardshorts

research_notes: No first-person interview with Gordon or Rena Merchant about 1973 could be found that loads (a 2017 Stab video interview has only a short description online), so the story states no feelings or thoughts and attributes each figure to its source. Where the shorts were made: Boardriders (the brand's own history) says the North Burleigh kitchen table; the International Directory of Company Histories says the kitchen table of a small rented apartment; the Encyclopedia of Surfing says the basement of their home at Burleigh Heads; recent Billabong marketing says a garage. The story gives the first two and the encyclopedia's version. How they sold: consignment to Gold Coast surf shops (IDCH) and from a vehicle while travelling (Encyclopedia of Surfing); both are given. The consignment price (A$4.50), first-year takings (A$5,000), the 1977 loan refusal, the A$7,500 loan in 1978 and the sales figures rest on the IDCH entry alone (Surfd and Reference for Business repeat the same text); they are attributed to it. The name: IDCH glosses billabong as 'oasis'; the V&A gives the Wiradjuri meaning of a creek that runs only in the rainy season, which the story uses. Who devised the triple stitch: Wikipedia credits Rena; Boardriders does not say; the story does not assign it. The 1972 bikini detail is from Boardriders only and is attributed to the company. Rena Merchant's later 49 per cent stake (bought by a consortium for A$24.6 million in 1998, per IDCH) is not used. Wikipedia is cited only as a supplementary cross-check for triple stitching. Funding: bootstrapped, supported by the IDCH account of no loan until 1978. The Encyclopedia of Surfing entries are partly behind a subscription; only their public opening sections were read and cited.
